Grid Spacing Dial

Number TheoryCoordinatesUnit Distance Problem
Game: A grid of dots is squeezed so that some neighbours end up exactly one step apart. Find the setting that makes the most pairs.
How to play: Turn the dial. The lines show the pairs that are exactly one step apart; the big purple dot shows where one dot's neighbours are. Tap the grid to move that dot.

Look for the math

Set the spacing of a square grid to 1/c, with c² a whole number. Two grid points are exactly 1 apart when their offset, in grid steps, is a pair (a, b) with a² + b² = c². So the dial picks which offsets count, and the number of offsets is the number of ways to write c² as a sum of two squares.

More ways, more neighbours, but a catch

Spacing 1 (c² = 1) has 4 offsets. c² = 25 has 12: (±5, 0), (0, ±5), (±3, ±4) and (±4, ±3). c² = 65 has 16. But an offset like (8, 1) only fits if the grid is wide enough, so pairs near the edge are lost. On a 16 × 16 grid, c² = 25 gives 976 unit pairs and c² = 65 only 912, though 65 has more offsets. The test checks both numbers by looking at every pair of points, and finds that 25 is the best choice for this grid.

The count

An offset (a, b) fits (k − |a|)(k − |b|) times in a k × k grid. Add that up over all offsets and halve it, because each pair is counted from both ends. Compare with a bigger grid and the best c² moves up: it pays to use richer c² when there is more room.

Why it is not enough

With n = k² points, the best c² gives about n · r₂(c²) / 2 pairs, and this can beat n by a factor that grows slower than any power of n. Erdős proved this gives n1 + C / log log n unit distances. Erdős conjectured that nothing could do much better than these grids, and that is the conjecture the 2026 construction disproved.

Change the grid size and find the best dial for each. Does the best c² grow with the grid?

An original game for coolmaths, after Paul Erdős's 1946 construction (Wikipedia)
